 The Trump administration has proposed tightening SNAP eligibility rules that could result in 6.3 million Americans losing food assistance, including potentially affecting West Virginia households, where roughly 272,800 residents receive benefits each month.
 Submitted Photo 
 CHARLESTON, W.Va. — Millions of Americans could lose access to federal food assistance under a new proposal from the Trump administration that would tighten eligibility requirements for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, adding another potential change to a program that has undergone significant federal revisions over the past year.
 The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed a rule Tuesday that would eliminate a policy allowing states to automatically extend SNAP eligibility to certain households receiving assistance through the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, commonly known as TANF.
 The USDA estimates the proposed change could result in approximately 6.3 million people losing SNAP benefits, representing nearly 18% of the program's current recipients. The agency's analysis projects the change would take full effect in fiscal year 2029.
 Under current policy, households receiving qualifying TANF assistance can become eligible for SNAP without having to meet the program's standard federal income and resource requirements. The practice, known as broad-based categorical eligibility, allows states to use participation in other assistance programs to streamline SNAP eligibility determinations and extend benefits to additional low-income households.
 The proposed rule would restrict that practice, requiring affected households to meet more standardized federal SNAP eligibility requirements.
